eras.boundary_note: No surveyed boundary lines exist for this era. The shaded region is an approximate depiction of the documented Wabanaki homeland (present-day Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and the Maritimes) — explicitly approximate, never empty or unclaimed.
eras.description: Before sustained European colonization, this region was the homeland of the Wabanaki peoples — the Mi'kmaq, Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet), Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, and Abenaki — who call it Wabanaki, 'Dawnland.' No European-drawn boundaries existed; the land was under Indigenous control. The Wabanaki homeland did not end in 1604 — Wabanaki presence, sovereignty, and resistance continued throughout the colonial period and to the present day, and the homeland is shown as a persistent background layer in later eras.
eras.label: Wabanaki Homelands

eras.boundary_note: These are overlapping paper claims, not settled boundary lines. Shown as translucent claim bands with their documented latitude and river anchors.
eras.description: France founded a settlement on Saint Croix Island in 1604 (moved to Port-Royal in 1605), claiming under the 1603 de Monts grant the coast between the 40th and 46th parallels. England countered with the Council for New England's November 1620 charter (40th to 48th parallel) and the 1622 Province of Maine patent between the Merrimack and Kennebec Rivers, plus the short-lived Popham Colony of 1607. The overlapping paper claims covered all of present-day Maine, though effective occupation on both sides was limited to scattered coastal posts.
eras.label: French Acadia vs. English Claims

eras.boundary_note: District extent is approximate — the interior remained under Wabanaki control. The Kennebec-to-St. Croix tract (granted to the Duke of York in 1669, administered as Cornwall County, New York) and French claims east of Penobscot Bay overlapped it and are shown as rival claim bands, not settled lines.
eras.description: Massachusetts Bay asserted jurisdiction over the Maine settlements in 1652, creating Yorkshire County from the Piscataqua River to Casco Bay, and had absorbed Gorges' Province of Maine and Lygonia by 1658. This was a contested claim, not settled rule: the Duke of York's competing 1669 grant of the Kennebec-to-St. Croix tract (the Territory of Sagadahock, administered as Cornwall County, Province of New York) was a separate rival jurisdiction, and France claimed lands east of Penobscot Bay as part of Acadia. The 1691 royal charter (effective 1692) folded all territory between the Piscataqua and St. Croix Rivers into the new Province of Massachusetts Bay. Maine remained part of Massachusetts until statehood in 1820.
eras.label: Massachusetts Claims & Rule

eras.boundary_note: The due-north line from the St. Croix source was surveyed and marked in 1817–1818 and is drawn as documented. The rival 'highlands' interpretations and the disputed zone between them are approximate — the highlands' identity was precisely what was disputed — and are labeled as rival claims, not a settled line. Southern and western boundaries follow the 1691 charter limits (Piscataqua to St. Croix), shown by the modern state outline.
eras.description: The 1783 Treaty of Paris defined the U.S.–British boundary from the source of the St. Croix River due north to the 'highlands' dividing St. Lawrence and Atlantic watersheds, then along those highlands to the northwesternmost head of the Connecticut River. The negotiators attached no map and the 'highlands' were never clearly identified, leaving roughly 7.7 million acres of northern Maine in dispute between rival American and British interpretations. Maine remained the District of Massachusetts throughout this period.
eras.label: Treaty of Paris Boundary Dispute

eras.description: Maine entered the Union as the 23rd state on March 15, 1820, under the Missouri Compromise, which admitted Maine as a free state alongside Missouri as a slave state. The northeastern boundary with New Brunswick remained unsettled, and rival Maine and New Brunswick timber operations in the disputed zone sparked the Aroostook 'War' of 1838–1839 — so called rhetorically; militias mobilized but never engaged in actual combat.
eras.label: State of Maine (Disputed North)

eras.boundary_note: The Webster–Ashburton line is the documented, settled northern boundary — the solid state outline shown on the map. Article I traces it from the St. Croix source monument north to the St. John, up the St. John and St. Francis to Lake Pohenegamook, then via survey lines to the highlands and down Hall's Stream to the 45th parallel.
eras.description: The Webster–Ashburton Treaty, signed August 9, 1842, in Washington, D.C., by Daniel Webster and Lord Ashburton, fixed the Maine–New Brunswick boundary and ended the 59-year dispute. It awarded most of the disputed territory to Maine while preserving an overland British connection between Lower Canada and the Maritime colonies. Maine's boundaries have been unchanged since. The Wabanaki nations — Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Mi'kmaq, and Wolastoqiyik — persist in Maine today; the Wabanaki Confederacy was revived in 1993.
eras.label: State of Maine

note: Territorial boundary/claim eras for the Maine Historical Atlas time slider. Coordinates are [lat, lng], matching sites.json convention. Every layer is labeled as either a surveyed/settled line or an APPROXIMATE reconstruction / paper claim — approximate geometry is never presented as a precise boundary. Sources verified September 2026.
slider_note: The in-app date slider operates at whole-year granularity, while some transitions have exact mid-year dates (Treaty of Paris, September 3 1783; Maine statehood, March 15 1820; Webster-Ashburton Treaty, August 9 1842). The eras' start_year/end_year boundaries are inclusive, so the slider assigns 1783 to the Massachusetts era, 1820 to the Treaty of Paris dispute era, and 1842 to the disputed-north era. Era descriptions carry the exact dates; the slider cannot distinguish months within a year.
